description: Georgia's historic "first bite rule" didn't mean quite what it sounds like. What an injured person had to prove, and when an owner is not liable.
shortAnswer: Though it may sound as if a dog had to have actually bitten a person in the past for an owner or keeper to be liable for injuries, that is not how the rule worked. What an injured person had to prove was that the animal had demonstrated a propensity to do the particular act that caused their injury.

faq.q: Under Georgia's first bite rule, did the dog's earlier incident have to be the same kind of attack?
faq.a: The prior incident did not have to involve identical acts as the acts that led to the later injury. But there did have to be evidence of vicious propensity, and the evidence that was required was a prior incident or incidents which would put a prudent person on notice to anticipate the event which occurred.

faq.q: Is a Georgia dog owner liable if the dog's past bite was provoked by teasing?
faq.a: An owner or keeper is not liable if the dog has bitten or attacked a person in the past but that bite or attack was provoked by teasing or other actions that incited the dog to attack.

faq.q: Is the rule different if the dog is part wolf?
faq.a: If a dog is part wolf or other wild animal, there is a different rule. In that instance there is legal authority for holding the owner or keeper strictly liable – which means the owner/keeper is responsible regardless of the animal's past history.

faq.q: Do the same rules apply to cat bites in Georgia?
faq.a: Since a cat is a domestic animal, cat bites or attacks are governed by the same set of rules as a dog.
